summary: Interlude response (GitLab Deletes Production). (1) Untested assumptions: I would bet the fork's own recovery path -- DB restores from pg_dump, the Celery worker restart under Redis loss, and the cache-rebuild path after a flush -- have never been exercised end to end; the redis RESP2 protocol override and graceful-degradation branches were only proven by code reading, not by actually killing Redis mid-request. Testing them today would likely surface the exact 'job runs but restore fails' class GitLab hit. (2) Class of mistake: destructive ops are one hostname away; our own setup has near-identical terminal windows for API/worker/tests, and a single `up -d`/cleanup command could hit the wrong DB. Safeguards: hostname-annotated prompts, a mandatory `psql -c "select pg_is_in_recovery()"` sanity gate before any destructive step, and dropping DBs only via a script that echoes the target first. (3) Radical transparency: GitLab gained trust and turned an outage into a reusable public case study; the risk was temporary reputation damage that honesty largely cancelled. My org's answer (public postmortem or not) would reveal whether we treat failure as a learning signal or as something to hide -- GitLab's own postmortem proves the former pays off.
